``` r
library(r2parquet)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

As an example we consider accessing dissemination block (DB) level geographic data from the 2021 Canadian census. For this we have prepared a parquet file in a public bucket, it can be reached by url.


``` r
census_db_url <- "https://data.mountainmath.xyz/census/2021/ldb_000b21f_e.parquet"
```

The data can be downloaded in full, but often we are interested in a specific part of Canada only, maybe a particular metro area (CMA) or census subdivision (CSD). The first step is to get a lazy connection to the parquet file.


``` r
db_table <- parquet_tbl(census_db_url)

db_table |> colnames()
#>  [1] "DBUID"    "DAUID"    "CTUID"    "CSDUID"   "CMAUID"   "CMAPUID" 
#>  [7] "CDUID"    "PRUID"    "DGUID"    "DBRPLAMX" "DBRPLAMY" "LANDAREA"
#> [13] "geometry"
```

This only reads the parquet metadata, the file carries several geographic identifiers as well as the geography. The table also carries custom metadata that gives more information about data provenance and licence.


``` r
db_table |> parquet_metadata()
#> $title
#> [1] "2021 Census – Boundary files - Dissemination blocks"
#> 
#> $source_url
#> [1] "https://www12.statcan.gc.ca/census-recensement/alternative_alternatif.cfm?l=eng&dispext=zip&teng=ldb_000b21f_e.zip&k=%20%20%20248570&loc=//www12.statcan.gc.ca/census-recensement/2021/geo/sip-pis/boundary-limites/files-fichiers/ldb_000b21f_e.zip"
#> 
#> $reference_guide
#> [1] "https://www12.statcan.gc.ca/census-recensement/2021/geo/ref/guide/index2021-eng.cfm?year=21"
#> 
#> $licence
#> [1] "Statistics Canada Open Licence"
#> 
#> $licence_url
#> [1] "https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/terms-conditions/open-licence"
#> 
#> $attribution
#> [1] "Statistics Canada Product ldb_000b21f_e"
```

A simple query would be to fetch the data for just the City of Vancouver.


``` r
data_csd <- db_table |>
  filter(CSDUID=="5915022") |>
  collect_parquet()

ggplot(data_csd) +
  geom_sf() +
  labs(title="City of Vancouver Dissemination Blocks",
       caption=parquet_metadata(data_csd)$attribution)
```

<div class="figure">
<img src="accessing_public_buckets-vancouver-csd-1.png" alt="plot of chunk vancouver-csd" width="100%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk vancouver-csd</p>
</div>

Similarly, we can fetch the data for Metro Vancouver. Both these queries run in less than a second because under the hood only the ranges for the data that's actually required are identified and read, with only limited unneeded data making the trip from R2 to the R session.


``` r
data_cma <- db_table |>
  filter(CMAUID=="933") |>
  collect_parquet()

ggplot(data_cma) +
  geom_sf() +
  labs(title="Metro Vancouver Dissemination Blocks",
       caption=parquet_metadata(data_cma)$attribution)
```

<div class="figure">
<img src="accessing_public_buckets-vancouver-cma-1.png" alt="plot of chunk vancouver-cma" width="100%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk vancouver-cma</p>
</div>

To build on this we query the geographic attributes hosted at


``` r
geo_attributes_path <- "https://data.mountainmath.xyz/census/2021/2021_92-151_X.parquet"
```

and read just the ones for Metro Vancouver.


``` r
geo_attributes <- parquet_tbl(geo_attributes_path) |>
  filter(CMAUID=="933") |>
  select(DBUID,Population=DBPOP2021) |>
  collect_parquet()
```

`collect_parquet()` works for tables without geometry too, and unlike `collect()` it attaches the file metadata, so the attribution of both sources can go into the caption.


``` r
data_cma |>
  left_join(geo_attributes, by="DBUID") |>
  mutate(density=Population/(LANDAREA*100)) |>
  mutate(density=if_else(is.finite(density),density,0)) |>
  mutate(bands=cut(density,breaks=c(-Inf,0,10,20,50,100,200,500,1000,Inf),
                   labels=c("0","0-10","10-20","20-50","50-100","100-200",
                            "200-500","500-1000",">1000"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(fill=bands)) +
  geom_sf(colour=NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma") +
  labs(title="Population density in Metro Vancouver",
       fill="Pop/ha",
       caption=paste0(parquet_metadata(data_cma)$attribution, " | ",
                      parquet_metadata(geo_attributes)$attribution))
```

<div class="figure">
<img src="accessing_public_buckets-vancouver-density-1.png" alt="plot of chunk vancouver-density" width="100%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk vancouver-density</p>
</div>



# Spatial queries

We can also use efficient spatial filtering when getting the data, for example querying data within a 10 km radius around central Toronto.


``` r
library(sf)
#> Linking to GEOS 3.13.0, GDAL 3.8.5, PROJ 9.5.1; sf_use_s2() is TRUE

mask <- st_point(c(-79.3842, 43.6514)) |> 
  st_sfc(crs = 4326) |>
  st_buffer(10000, max_cells = 10000) 

data_mask <- db_table |>
  filter_spatial(mask) |>
  collect_parquet()

data_mask |>
  st_set_agr("constant") |>
  st_intersection(mask |> st_transform(st_crs(data_mask))) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf() +
  labs(title="Dissemination blocks in central Toronto",
       caption=parquet_metadata(data_mask)$attribution) 
```

<div class="figure">
<img src="accessing_public_buckets-toronto-radius-1.png" alt="plot of chunk toronto-radius" width="100%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk toronto-radius</p>
</div>

The `filter_spatial` function returns every feature that intersects the mask, clipping the returned data with `st_intersection` makes for a prettier plot. `filter_spatial()` transforms the mask to the crs of the data automatically, `st_intersection()` needs the explicit transformation.
